notes.title: Unsupervised Rhythm and Voice Conversion to Improve ASR on Dysarthric Speech
notes.bp: ASR should recover dysarthric speech even when slow rhythm and unusual voice quality make the acoustic pattern unlike healthy training speech.
notes.wh: Speaker variation and rate changes are entangled, and a conversion that sounds healthier may alter linguistic content or fail for severe dysarthria.
notes.naive: Apply a generic speed perturbation or train a speaker-specific converter and assume the recognizer will adapt.
notes.ap: Use unsupervised rhythm and voice conversion with syllable-level rhythm modeling, then measure whether converted speech helps LF-MMI and Whisper ASR.
notes.mech: RnV converts timing and voice characteristics without parallel healthy speech; syllable structure supplies a dysarthria-relevant rhythm representation before ASR scoring.
notes.math: Conversion is a task-conditioned invariance: remove cues that obstruct recognition while retaining phonetic content needed by the recognizer.
notes.eval: Conversion is a task-conditioned invariance: remove cues that obstruct recognition while retaining phonetic content needed by the recognizer.
notes.ww: On Torgo, LF-MMI shows reported WER reductions, especially for severe dysarthria, while Whisper fine-tuning on converted data has minimal effect.
notes.limits: Torgo speakers, severity, conversion fidelity, ASR backend, and WER protocol bound transfer; improved recognition is not improved naturalness or clinical communication.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Vo-Ve: An Explainable Voice-Vector for Speaker Identity Evaluation
notes.bp: A speaker-similarity system should say not only whether two voices match but which voice attributes support that judgment.
notes.wh: Ordinary embeddings compress identity into opaque coordinates, making errors and shifts across tasks difficult to interpret.
notes.naive: Use a black-box speaker embedding and treat its similarity score as a complete explanation.
notes.ap: Represent identity with an interpretable vector of explicit voice-attribute class probabilities and compare its similarity with conventional embeddings.
notes.mech: Vo-Ve maps speech to attribute probabilities; similarity can then be decomposed into human-readable properties instead of a single latent distance.
notes.math: The representation trades some compact opacity for an interpretable coordinate system whose attributes can be inspected when similarity changes.
notes.eval: The representation trades some compact opacity for an interpretable coordinate system whose attributes can be inspected when similarity changes.
notes.ww: The paper reports competitive speaker-similarity evaluation and attribute-level explanations in its experiments.
notes.limits: Attribute inventory, labels, language, channel variation, and metric protocol bound interpretability; explainable similarity is not proof of causal identity factors.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Bidirectional Spoken-Written Text Conversion with Large Language Models
notes.bp: A recognizer should handle both spoken-form and written-form transcripts without inconsistent normalization of numbers, names, or punctuation.
notes.wh: Speech databases often contain one transcription convention while modern models emit another, and manually building paired forms is expensive.
notes.naive: Train on whichever transcript convention is available or attach a one-way text-normalization postprocessor.
notes.ap: Use LLM-generated dual transcriptions, iterative supervised/semi-supervised expansion, and a bidirectional text-conversion model supporting both ITN and TN.
notes.mech: The model learns mappings in both directions; generated paired text supplies supervision while iterative learning enlarges the conversion data.
notes.math: The central object is a representation boundary between spoken language and written conventions, not a change to the acoustic evidence itself.
notes.eval: The central object is a representation boundary between spoken language and written conventions, not a change to the acoustic evidence itself.
notes.ww: The paper reports a 13.4% ERR improvement in the evaluated conversion setting.
notes.limits: LLM generation quality, language conventions, error metric, transcript domain, and iterative-label bias bound transfer; normalization success is not ASR acoustic accuracy.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Who knows best? Effects of speech disfluencies on incentivized decision-making
notes.bp: Listeners may use pauses and disfluencies as evidence when deciding whom or what to believe, so removing them can change behavior rather than merely readability.
notes.wh: Prior ratings of competence do not show whether speech cues affect consequential choices, and credibility judgments interact with source conflict and incentives.
notes.naive: Normalize all disfluent speech before evaluation or infer real-world behavior from Likert ratings alone.
notes.ap: Use an incentivized web decision task with conflicting information and compare choices as a function of speech fluency.
notes.mech: The experiment treats disfluency as part of the observed communication signal and measures choice behavior rather than only an attitude rating.
notes.math: Behavioral choice is a downstream proxy: it tests whether a listener’s interpretation of fluency changes action under incentives.
notes.eval: Behavioral choice is a downstream proxy: it tests whether a listener’s interpretation of fluency changes action under incentives.
notes.ww: The study reports that listeners take speech fluency into account when deciding whom or what to believe.
notes.limits: Task stakes, speakers, disfluency types, online sample, and source-conflict design bound transfer; choice bias is not proof that disfluencies carry truthful information.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: NanoCodec: Towards High-Quality Ultra Fast Speech LLM Inference
notes.bp: A speech codec used inside an autoregressive audio model should compress sound with few tokens per second without destroying reconstruction quality.
notes.wh: High frame rates make every generated second expensive, while lowering rate or bitrate can erase fine acoustic detail and causality can add delay.
notes.naive: Choose a low frame rate without measuring the rate/bitrate/causality tradeoff, or optimize only waveform quality at an impractical token rate.
notes.ap: Ablate frame rate, bitrate, and causality, then design NanoCodec around a low-rate operating point and compare reconstruction quality.
notes.mech: The codec maps audio to discrete tokens and back; token rate controls autoregressive steps while bitrate and causal context control information and latency.
notes.math: Compression is a rate-distortion-resource tradeoff: fewer symbols reduce computation but constrain what the decoder can reconstruct.
notes.eval: Compression is a rate-distortion-resource tradeoff: fewer symbols reduce computation but constrain what the decoder can reconstruct.
notes.ww: NanoCodec reports high-quality compression at 12.5 FPS and competitive results across bitrate ranges.
notes.limits: Audio domain, codec training data, perceptual metric, hardware, and causality setting bound transfer; codec quality is not end-to-end speech generation quality.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Improving Generalization of End-to-End ASR through Diversity and Independence Regularization
notes.bp: An ASR model should generalize when test speech differs from training speech instead of memorizing redundant or narrow feature patterns.
notes.wh: CTC, AED, and RNN-T models can overfit in different ways, and increasing feature diversity without controlling redundancy may not help.
notes.naive: Add capacity or regularize all features identically without identifying whether redundancy or lack of diversity causes the error.
notes.ap: Add diversity loss to separate feature representations and independence loss to reduce covariance, then test across three ASR architectures.
notes.mech: The losses operate on learned feature vectors: one discourages collapse toward similar patterns, the other discourages redundant correlated dimensions.
notes.math: The method shapes representation geometry so multiple informative directions survive while redundant variation is suppressed.
notes.eval: The method shapes representation geometry so multiple informative directions survive while redundant variation is suppressed.
notes.ww: The paper reports improved generalization and robustness for CTC, AED, and RNN-T models in the evaluated tasks.
notes.limits: Training/test shifts, loss weights, architectures, languages, and robustness protocol bound transfer; benchmark generalization is not immunity to arbitrary distribution shift.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: You Are What You Say: Exploiting Linguistic Content for VoicePrivacy Attacks
notes.bp: A voice-privacy attack should not mistake repeated linguistic content for speaker identity when evaluating anonymization.
notes.wh: If attacker training and test utterances share semantic or lexical content, text alone can predict the speaker and make privacy scores misleading.
notes.naive: Use a standard ASV attack and assume its error reflects only acoustic identity leakage.
notes.ap: Adapt BERT to attack speaker identity from transcript content, inspect explainable keywords, and compare the resulting EER and dataset construction.
notes.mech: The attacker maps linguistic content to speaker labels; semantically similar utterances become a non-acoustic identity channel in the evaluation.
notes.math: Privacy evaluation requires separating nuisance correlations from the protected attribute; otherwise the attack measures corpus curation rather than voice leakage.
notes.eval: Privacy evaluation requires separating nuisance correlations from the protected attribute; otherwise the attack measures corpus curation rather than voice leakage.
notes.ww: The paper reports mean EER around 35%, with some speakers as low as 2%, using text alone on VoicePrivacy data.
notes.limits: Dataset curation, speaker/content overlap, BERT training, split design, and EER interpretation bound the claim; text leakage does not prove an anonymizer fails acoustically.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Variability in performance across four generations of automatic speaker recognition systems
notes.bp: A speaker-recognition benchmark should reveal which people and conditions remain difficult, not only report one aggregate score across model generations.
notes.wh: Architectural improvements can hide persistent speaker-level failures, and file-level factors can be confused with stable person-level difficulty.
notes.naive: Compare only aggregate metrics or assume each new generation improves every speaker equally.
notes.ap: Evaluate four generations on the same forensic test/calibration data at both system and individual-speaker levels.
notes.mech: Matched evaluation separates model-generation effects from test-set changes and decomposes variation by file and speaker factors.
notes.math: The unit of analysis matters: an overall metric averages heterogeneous difficulty, while per-speaker outcomes expose persistent tails.
notes.eval: The unit of analysis matters: an overall metric averages heterogeneous difficulty, while per-speaker outcomes expose persistent tails.
notes.ww: Performance improves from GMM-UBM through i-vector and x-vector but not ECAPA-TDNN in the reported comparison; some individuals remain difficult across systems.
notes.limits: Forensic data, calibration, system implementations, speaker sampling, and metric choice bound transfer; persistent difficulty is not automatically a biological property.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.
